sources.title: Interview — Internal Medicine Resident on Opting In to the Scribe
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-27 review of the internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:26-27) found attending physicians opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments (same file, :37-39). It recommended a short follow-up interview round on the physician/resident adoption gap (same file, :44) and asked whether the gap is explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else, which dashboard data alone can't answer (same file, :47-48). No other raw session dated on or before this one mentions residents (the only matches are that file's :38, :44 and :47), and no earlier session interviewed a resident. This session asked one internal medicine resident, about nine months after the January 2026 GA, when and why they opted in to the ambient scribe. It is one resident's account and can't explain the gap the dashboard showed. Phase 4 has no inpatient, ED or behavioral health sessions, so whether and how residents use the scribe in those settings stays an open gap.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine resident who sees patients in an ambulatory internal medicine clinic on set half-days. They opted in to the ambient scribe in spring 2026, some months after the January 2026 GA, and use it for some of their clinic visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; they review the draft, correct single lines in place, and sign. How attendings review resident notes was not discussed. Only clinic visits were discussed. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (waiting) They did not opt in at GA. In their account, writing their own notes in their first months in clinic was how they worked out their assessment of a patient, and they did not want a draft doing that for them while they were still learning it. They did not describe doubts about the draft's accuracy as the reason. This is one resident's reason; whether other residents waited for the same reason is not known.
[MEDIUM] (opting in) They opted in once they felt settled in writing notes and wanted to keep up on half-days that ran late. They put that at "about three months into clinic", an informal recollection.
[MEDIUM] (which visits) They use the scribe mostly for follow-up visits on problems they already know. For a new problem they write the assessment themselves, or rewrite the draft's assessment before signing. That is their description of their own practice; how often they do each was not discussed.
[LOW] (how they heard) What they knew about the scribe before opting in came from seeing attendings in their clinic use it. They did not know of any training or introduction aimed at residents.
Representative Quotes
"Writing the assessment is how I work out what I think. I didn't want something else writing it while I was still learning that." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
"For a follow-up on a problem I know, the draft is fine. A new problem, I still write the assessment myself." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
Recommendations
When resident adoption is next looked at, ask about note writing as part of training alongside workflow and trust; this resident's reason for waiting was learning to write notes, and they did not describe doubt about the draft's accuracy as a reason.
Interview more residents, including in other departments, before drawing conclusions about the adoption gap; this is one resident.
Record how residents are offered the scribe and any training for them; no raw session dated on or before this one records it.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why residents opted in at a lower rate than attendings in the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout, as the dashboard review recorded (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:27, :37-39), is still not known; one resident's account can't explain it.
Whether residents use the scribe in inpatient, ED or behavioral health settings is not known; Phase 4 has no sessions in those settings, and the gap stays open.
How attendings review scribe-drafted resident notes was not discussed, and no raw session dated on or before this one records it.

runs.answer:
The adoption data covers the first 4 weeks of the ambient scribe's GA-candidate rollout, taken from an internal analytics dashboard [1]. Priya Patel reviewed that dashboard manually, with no moderated session and no participants, in a review dated January 27, 2026 [1]. A topline summary dated January 28, 2026 reports the same 4-week window from that review [2].

The sources do not give the exact start and end dates of the 4 weeks. Elsewhere, GA is recorded as coming in January 2026 [3].

The 4-week window showed two patterns:
- Clinicians shown per-line confidence highlighting skimmed high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort [1]. This matches the January 2026 usability round, where 4 of 6 participants said the highlighting let them skim high-confidence lines for the first time [4].
- Attending physicians opted in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments [1]. The review said dashboard data alone can't explain this gap [1].

A later interview with one internal medicine resident (P153), about nine months after GA, followed up on that adoption gap [5]. It still describes the gap as covering "the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout" [5]. That resident waited about three months into clinic before opting in, because writing their own notes was how they learned to work out an assessment [5].

The 2026-01-27 review of the internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:26-27) found attending physicians opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments (same file, :37-39). It recommended a short follow-up interview round on the physician/resident adoption gap (same file, :44) and asked whether the gap is explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else, which dashboard data alone can't answer (same file, :47-48). No other raw session dated on or before this one mentions residents (the only matches are that file's :38, :44 and :47), and no earlier session interviewed a resident. This session asked one internal medicine resident, about nine months after the January 2026 GA, when and why they opted in to the ambient scribe. It is one resident's account and can't explain the gap the dashboard showed. Phase 4 has no inpatient, ED or behavioral health sessions, so whether and how residents use the scribe in those settings stays an open gap.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine resident who sees patients in an ambulatory internal medicine clinic on set half-days. They opted in to the ambient scribe in spring 2026, some months after the January 2026 GA, and use it for some of their clinic visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; they review the draft, correct single lines in place, and sign. How attendings review resident notes was not discussed. Only clinic visits were discussed. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (waiting) They did not opt in at GA. In their account, writing their own notes in their first months in clinic was how they worked out their assessment of a patient, and they did not want a draft doing that for them while they were still learning it. They did not describe doubts about the draft's accuracy as the reason. This is one resident's reason; whether other residents waited for the same reason is not known.
[MEDIUM] (opting in) They opted in once they felt settled in writing notes and wanted to keep up on half-days that ran late. They put that at "about three months into clinic", an informal recollection.
[MEDIUM] (which visits) They use the scribe mostly for follow-up visits on problems they already know. For a new problem they write the assessment themselves, or rewrite the draft's assessment before signing. That is their description of their own practice; how often they do each was not discussed.
[LOW] (how they heard) What they knew about the scribe before opting in came from seeing attendings in their clinic use it. They did not know of any training or introduction aimed at residents.
Representative Quotes
"Writing the assessment is how I work out what I think. I didn't want something else writing it while I was still learning that." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
"For a follow-up on a problem I know, the draft is fine. A new problem, I still write the assessment myself." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
Recommendations
When resident adoption is next looked at, ask about note writing as part of training alongside workflow and trust; this resident's reason for waiting was learning to write notes, and they did not describe doubt about the draft's accuracy as a reason.
Interview more residents, including in other departments, before drawing conclusions about the adoption gap; this is one resident.
Record how residents are offered the scribe and any training for them; no raw session dated on or before this one records it.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why residents opted in at a lower rate than attendings in the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout, as the dashboard review recorded (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:27, :37-39), is still not known; one resident's account can't explain it.
Whether residents use the scribe in inpatient, ED or behavioral health settings is not known; Phase 4 has no sessions in those settings, and the gap stays open.
How attendings review scribe-drafted resident notes was not discussed, and no raw session dated on or before this one records it.

runs.answer:
The ambient scribe adoption data covers the first 4 weeks of the GA-candidate rollout, taken from an internal analytics dashboard [1]. Researcher Priya Patel reviewed it manually on January 27, 2026, with no moderated session or participants [1]. The January 28, 2026 topline summary is based on that same review and states the same 4-week window [2].

The sources do not give exact start and end dates for those 4 weeks. For context, the final pre-GA usability test ran on January 13, 2026 [3], and GA itself came in January 2026 [4].

Within that window, the data showed two things:

- Clinicians shown confidence highlighting skimmed high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort [1].
- Attending physicians opted in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments [1].

The later October 2026 interview with an internal medicine resident (P153) is not part of this dataset. It was a qualitative follow-up on the attending/resident gap, conducted about nine months after GA [5]. It is explicitly one resident's account and cannot explain the gap the dashboard showed [5].

sources.title: Dashboard review — Ambient scribe GA candidate adoption
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the ambient scribe GA release candidate to see whether adoption and engagement patterns in real usage match what the GA-candidate usability round found — particularly whether the per-line confidence highlighting is actually changing reviewing behavior at scale, not just in the moderated session.
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (trust) Clinicians who were shown confidence highlighting skim high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort — directionally consistent with the usability round's finding that visible uncertainty, not raw accuracy, changes reviewing behavior.
[LOW] (adoption) Adoption is uneven by role: attending physicians are opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments, worth understanding qualitatively rather than assuming it's a training gap.
Recommendations
Feed this dashboard pattern back into findings/ambient-scribe.md as corroborating evidence for the confidence-highlighting result, rather than treating it as a separate finding.
Consider a short follow-up interview round specifically on the physician/resident adoption gap.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Is the physician/resident adoption gap explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else entirely? Dashboard data alone can't answer this.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient AI Scribe GA Release Candidate (Final Validation)
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Final validation pass on the ambient scribe before GA release, testing the v0.3 confidence-indicator concept (from September's recommendation) and confirming readiness against the full history of prior findings.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, simulated + 2 real (consented) low-acuity encounters, 45 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[LOW] (confidence indicator (positive)) The new per-line confidence highlighting (low-confidence transcription shown in a subtle underline) was well received and, notably, 4 of 6 participants said it let them skim high-confidence lines for the first time across the whole testing history — the first session where reduced line-by-line reading was observed.
[MEDIUM] (sound-alike medication errors) Still present in 1 of 6 sessions despite the pronunciation dictionary work referenced in September; team should treat this as an ongoing monitoring item post-GA rather than a pre-GA blocker, given the confidence indicator now flags it for review anyway.
[MEDIUM] (training readiness) Participants who'd been through the champion-model style training pilot (per October's recommendation) reported higher initial comfort than those who hadn't, though this wasn't a controlled comparison.
[LOW] (phi-handling (confirmed stable)) Draft-retention/auto-expiry behavior (fixed in v0.2) remains stable and correctly documented for audit purposes; no new PHI-handling issues found.
Representative Quotes
"This is the first time I actually skimmed a section instead of reading every word, because it showed me exactly where to look instead." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from v0.1 and v0.2)
"I went through the champion training last month and honestly walked in already comfortable. That part worked." — Nurse Practitioner, P118 (new participant)
Recommendations
Approve for GA release; the critical (Feb) and high (Feb, Sept) findings across this tool's full testing history are resolved or actively monitored, and the confidence-indicator concept appears to be the trust-building lever the team was looking for since September.
Continue tracking sound-alike medication errors as a post-GA metric rather than delaying release further for a low-frequency, now-flagged issue.
Use this session as the evidence base for the CIO's requested 'documentation time saved' 2026 headline metric baseline measurement.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Set up post-GA monitoring dashboard for sound-alike medication error rate.
Feed this session's time data into the formal 2026 metrics document (per December retro action item).

questions.question: What percentage of clinicians report burnout?

runs.answer:
The sources don't give a percentage of clinicians who report burnout, only figures on what drives it and on after-hours charting, mostly for physicians.

- The September 2025 baseline survey of 287 physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants and registered nurses included a validated burnout subscale [1]. The notes don't report an overall burnout rate from it [1].
- Among physicians, 52% chose documentation burden as their top contributor to burnout, ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. This figure ranks causes and doesn't show how many physicians are burned out [1].
- 64% of physician respondents reported regularly finishing documentation after clinic hours, averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours a day [1][2].
- The survey's roster includes registered nurses, but its notes report the burnout and after-hours figures for physicians only, and whether nurse results exist isn't recorded [3]. The physician figures shouldn't be read as describing nurses [3].
- Respondents were told the survey related to a future AI initiative, which may have primed their answers. Any comparison with the February nursing survey needs to account for this [1][2].
- One night-shift nurse described charting 30 to 45 minutes after most shifts and linked it to fatigue rather than burnout. No burnout measure was used in that interview [3].
- The recommended six-month repeat of the baseline survey isn't recorded, so any change since the January 2026 scribe rollout hasn't been measured [4].

sources.title: Survey — Clinician Burnout & Documentation Burden Baseline
sources.participants: Participants: 287 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Establish a pre-AI-rollout baseline of self-reported burnout and documentation burden, so future surveys can measure whether Compass AI tools move the needle.
Method
Method: Anonymous org-wide survey, 15 questions (validated burnout subscale + custom documentation items)
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.
[MEDIUM] (baseline caution) Respondents were told this survey relates to a future AI initiative, which may have primed more favorable-than-baseline attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools — worth noting as a methodological caveat for anyone comparing to the February nursing survey, which didn't mention AI in its framing.
Representative Quotes
"I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." — Physician, P84 (survey open-ended)
"Just don't let 'AI will fix documentation' become the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it." — Nurse Practitioner, P91 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Use this survey as the official baseline metric for measuring Compass AI's impact on documentation burden and after-hours charting in future re-surveys (e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout).
Note the framing caveat explicitly in any report comparing this dataset to the February nursing survey.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Schedule a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout for comparison.

sources.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
sources.excerpt: Documentation burden is real and quantifiable, not just anecdotal. The September baseline found documentation burden is physicians' #1 self-selected burnout driver (52%, ahead of patient volume at 31%), with 64% doing regular after-hours "pajama time" charting (avg. 1.2 hrs/day). The session recommends it as the official pre-AI baseline for measuring Compass AI's impact at 6 and 12 months post-rollout. Caveat: the September survey mentioned the AI initiative explicitly in its framing, while the February survey didn't — any comparison between the two datasets needs to account for that framing difference, not treat them as a clean before/after.

sources.title: Interview — Med-Surg Night Nurse on Charting Load
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The documentation-burden finding quantifies after-hours charting for physicians only: the September 2025 baseline found 64% of physician respondents regularly finishing documentation after clinic hours, at a self-reported 1.2 hours a day (2025-09-09-survey-clinician-burnout-documentation-burden-baseline/session-notes.md:30). Nothing in the corpus describes the same thing for nurses beyond the February 2025 nursing survey's attitudes and one respondent's wish to get "out of the room 10 minutes faster to chart" (2025-02-11-survey-nursing-attitudes-ai-documentation/session-notes.md:37). This session asked an inpatient nurse whether their charting runs past the end of their shift, why, and what they expect of AI drafting nursing notes, which doesn't exist.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a registered nurse on an inpatient medical-surgical unit, working twelve-hour night shifts, about two years in; they finished unit orientation as a new graduate. Their charting is manual. The ambient scribe, GA since January 2026, drafts notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only, and no nurse uses it for their own documentation, so everything they said about AI drafting nursing notes is an expectation, not experience. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the February 2025 nursing survey.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (after-shift charting) Their charting regularly continues after the shift ends. They hand off at the end of the night, then stay at a workstation to finish notes they could not complete during the shift. They put it at "most shifts, thirty to forty-five minutes"; that is an informal self-estimate, not timed or logged. The notes left over are mostly the narrative parts and the end-of-shift reassessments, because the start of the night is admissions and the early morning is medication passes and labs, and charting is what gets deferred whenever a patient needs something.
[MEDIUM] (burden beyond physicians) This extends the documentation-burden finding to registered nurses qualitatively: one nurse describes after-shift charting as routine on their unit. It does not supply a nurse figure. The September 2025 figures (52%, 64%, 1.2 hours a day) are physician-only and should not be read as describing nurses; this interview's thirty to forty-five minutes is one nurse's estimate and isn't comparable to them. They linked the after-shift time to how tired they are at the end of a run of nights, but described it as fatigue, not burnout, and no burnout measure was used.
[LOW] (tenure and skepticism) Asked about years of experience, they offered their own view as a newer nurse: they haven't settled into a way of charting yet, which might make them more open to a draft, but it also means they would check every word, because they don't yet trust themselves to spot what a draft got wrong. This is one newer nurse's view. It does not answer the February 2025 survey's open question on whether skepticism correlates with tenure, which needs the survey cross-tab.
Representative Quotes
"Report's done and I'm still at the workstation finishing my notes. Day shift is already running the floor around me." — Registered Nurse (medical-surgical), P141
"I'm new enough that I don't have a way of charting yet. Maybe that makes me more open to it. It also means I'd read every word, because I don't trust myself to know what it got wrong." — Registered Nurse (medical-surgical), P141
Recommendations
When the documentation-burden finding is next revised, note that after-shift charting is also reported by nurses, qualitatively, and keep the September figures labelled as physician-only.
If nurse documentation burden needs a number, measure it directly (the September baseline's registered nurse responses reported separately, if they exist, or time logs), rather than extending the physician figures.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How much time nurses spend charting after their shift is not measured; "thirty to forty-five minutes" is one nurse's estimate, on one unit.
The September 2025 baseline's roster lists registered nurses among its respondents, but its notes report the burnout and after-hours figures for physicians only; whether nurse results exist is not recorded.
Whether skepticism varies with tenure is still open; the February 2025 survey's cross-tab hasn't been run, and one interview can't answer it.
Whether day-shift nurses on the same unit chart after their shift too is not known.

sources.title: Interview — Family Physician on After-Hours Charting Since GA
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The September 2025 baseline survey asked about after-hours charting and reported it for physician respondents (2025-09-09-survey-clinician-burnout-documentation-burden-baseline/session-notes.md:29). It recommended future re-surveys "(e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout)" (same file, :40) and listed as a follow-up "a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout" (same file, :44). No repeat is recorded in research/raw on or before this session's date: the only survey folder after September 2025 is the December 2025 all-staff AI readiness pulse (2025-12-02-survey-allstaff-ai-readiness-pulse). No earlier 1:1 session asked a physician about charting after clinic: among raw sessions dated on or before 2026-07-02, after-hours and "pajama time" charting appear only in the September survey (session-notes.md:29, :40). This session asked a family physician, about six months after the January 2026 GA, when and how they finish their notes now. It is one physician's informal account and does not re-measure anything the survey measured.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a family medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about ten years in practice. They opted in to the ambient scribe shortly after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs, and enters orders separately. They did not take part in any earlier session; whether they responded to the September 2025 survey is not known, because it was anonymous. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed, and nothing was timed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (evening notes) They still finish some notes after clinic on most days. In their account the evening work is now mostly reading and signing drafts they didn't get to between visits, plus the notes for visits where they chose not to use the scribe; before the scribe, they recalled, it was mostly writing notes from memory. They put it at "four or five notes on a full day", an informal estimate. They have not timed it, then or now, and this is not a measure of time saved.
[MEDIUM] (which notes wait) The drafts that wait until the evening are the ones that need more than a quick read: long visits with several problems, and drafts where they expect to move or rewrite lines. Short visits they try to sign straight after the patient leaves. When the clinic runs late, that falls apart and more drafts wait.
[MEDIUM] (reviewing later) Reviewing a draft hours after the visit is harder for them than reviewing it straight away, because checking it depends on remembering what was said. In the evening they read more slowly and leave more of it as written when they can't recall the detail. That is their own description of their practice; how often it happens was not discussed.
[LOW] (other evening work) They said much of their evening now goes to patient messages and test results rather than notes, and the scribe doesn't touch those. That is their impression; how their evening time divides was not measured.
Representative Quotes
"The evening used to be writing. Now it's mostly reading what it wrote and signing, and then the messages." — Physician (Family Medicine), P150
"Right after the visit I remember what we said. By the evening I'm checking it against a memory that's gone fuzzy." — Physician (Family Medicine), P150
Recommendations
Treat this interview as context for the repeat of the September 2025 survey, not as a measure. Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA needs that repeat, which the baseline recommended and which is not recorded in the corpus.
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, a draft reviewed hours after the visit gets a weaker check, because the check depends on memory of the visit.
In later after-hours questions, ask about patient messages and test results as well as notes, since this physician placed much of their evening work there.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA is not measured; this is one physician's informal account, and no repeat of the September 2025 survey is recorded in the corpus.
How their evening time divides between notes, messages and results is not measured.
Whether other physicians, or NPs and PAs, describe the same pattern is not known; this is one interview.

runs.answer:
The sources do not give a percentage of clinicians who report burnout. The September 2025 baseline survey included a validated burnout subscale, but its recorded findings do not report an overall burnout rate [1].

What the sources do show:

- Among physicians, 52% chose documentation burden as their top contributor to burnout, ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. This is the share naming a cause, not the share reporting burnout [1].
- 64% of physician respondents said they regularly finish documentation after clinic hours, at a self-reported average of 1.2 hours a day [1].
- The survey had 287 respondents, including nurse practitioners, physician assistants and registered nurses, but these figures are reported for physicians only [1]. Whether results for the other groups exist is not recorded [2].
- The survey told respondents it related to a future AI initiative, which may have influenced their answers [1]. Comparisons with the February 2025 nursing survey need to account for that difference [3].
- One med-surg night nurse (P141) said their charting runs "thirty to forty-five minutes" past the end of most shifts [2]. They called this fatigue rather than burnout, and no burnout measure was used [2].
- About six months after the January 2026 ambient scribe launch, one family physician (P150) still finishes "four or five notes on a full day" after clinic, by their own informal estimate [4]. No repeat of the September survey is recorded, so any change in after-hours charting has not been measured [4].

sources.title: Interview — Family Physician on After-Hours Charting Since GA
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The September 2025 baseline survey asked about after-hours charting and reported it for physician respondents (2025-09-09-survey-clinician-burnout-documentation-burden-baseline/session-notes.md:29). It recommended future re-surveys "(e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout)" (same file, :40) and listed as a follow-up "a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout" (same file, :44). No earlier 1:1 session asked a physician about charting after clinic: among raw sessions dated on or before 2026-07-02, after-hours and "pajama time" charting appear only in the September survey (session-notes.md:29, :40). This session asked a family physician, about six months after the January 2026 GA, when and how they finish their notes now. It is one physician's informal account and does not re-measure anything the survey measured.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a family medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about ten years in practice. They opted in to the ambient scribe shortly after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. They did not take part in any earlier session; whether they responded to the September 2025 survey is not known, because it was anonymous. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed, and nothing was timed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (evening notes) They still finish some notes after clinic on most days. In their account the evening work is now mostly reading and signing drafts they didn't get to between visits, plus the notes for visits where they chose not to use the scribe; before the scribe, they recalled, it was mostly writing notes from memory. They put it at "four or five notes on a full day", an informal estimate. They have not timed it, then or now, and this is not a measure of time saved.
[MEDIUM] (which notes wait) The drafts that wait until the evening are the ones that need more than a quick read: long visits with several problems, and drafts where they expect to move or rewrite lines. Short visits they try to sign straight after the patient leaves. When the clinic runs late, that falls apart and more drafts wait.

Treat this interview as context for the repeat of the September 2025 survey, not as a measure. Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA needs that repeat, which the baseline recommended and which is not recorded in the corpus.

Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA is not measured; this is one physician's informal account, and no repeat of the September 2025 survey is recorded in the corpus.
How their evening time divides between notes, messages and results is not measured.
Whether other physicians, or NPs and PAs, describe the same pattern is not known; this is one interview.

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

runs.answer:
Awareness differed sharply between clinical and non-clinical staff. In the December 2, 2025 all-staff AI Readiness Pulse Survey (421 anonymous respondents, 10 questions), only 34% of non-clinical staff said they were aware that Compass AI initiatives were underway at all, compared with 71% of clinical staff [1]. The survey rated this finding medium confidence and suggested that internal communications had been focused on clinical staff [1].

One non-clinical/administrative respondent described the gap in an open-ended answer: "I hear about this AI stuff from clinical friends but nobody's told admin staff what's actually happening or if it affects us." (P112) [1]

The researcher recommended broadening Compass AI communications to non-clinical staff before any admin-facing pilot, such as a scheduling chatbot, goes live [1]. This matters because "appointment scheduling help" was the top write-in feature request among non-clinical/admin staff, while clinical staff still chose "documentation time savings" first [1].

Among clinical respondents, favorable sentiment toward AI-assisted documentation was somewhat higher than in an earlier baseline period [1]. However, the survey used different question wording from February's, so this is directional context rather than a clean comparison [1].

sources.title: Survey — All-Staff AI Readiness Pulse Survey
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Take an org-wide temperature check on AI readiness/sentiment heading into 2026, as input to roadmap prioritization and communications planning.
Method
Method: Org-wide anonymous pulse survey, 10 questions
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (awareness gap) Only 34% of non-clinical staff reported being aware Compass AI initiatives were underway at all, versus 71% of clinical staff — suggesting internal communications have been clinically focused and may need broadening if non-clinical rollouts (e.g., scheduling) proceed.
[MEDIUM] (sentiment trend (directional, not causal)) Among clinical respondents, favorable sentiment toward AI-assisted documentation was somewhat higher than the March-ish baseline period, though this survey used different question wording than February's, so it's directional context rather than a clean comparison.
[LOW] (top requested feature) When asked what AI feature they'd most want next, 'appointment scheduling help' was the top write-in among non-clinical/admin staff, and 'documentation time savings' remained the top pick among clinical staff — consistent with priorities identified all year.
Representative Quotes
"I hear about this AI stuff from clinical friends but nobody's told admin staff what's actually happening or if it affects us." — Non-clinical/administrative staff, P112 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Broaden internal communications about Compass AI to non-clinical staff specifically before any admin-facing pilot (e.g., scheduling chatbot) goes live, given the awareness gap found here.
If a clean sentiment trend is wanted for 2026 reporting, re-run the exact February nursing survey instrument rather than a new pulse survey, to get a true apples-to-apples comparison.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Decide with leadership whether the September burnout survey or a repeat of the February survey is the better instrument for the planned 6-month post-GA comparison.

sources.title: AI Strategy Kickoff — Executive Alignment Interview
sources.participants: Participants: 2 — Chief Information Officer ×1, VP Clinical Informatics ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand executive priorities, risk tolerance, and success criteria for the Compass AI modernization program before any tools are scoped.
Method
Method: 1:1 stakeholder interview (60 min, recorded w/ consent, transcript scrubbed)
Researcher: J. Alvarez
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (risk tolerance) Both stakeholders want AI pilots to start in low-PHI-exposure workflows (scheduling, intake) before touching clinical documentation, citing HIPAA audit exposure as the top concern.
[MEDIUM] (success criteria) VP Clinical Informatics defines success as 'reduced documentation time,' while CIO defines success as 'reduced vendor sprawl' — the two are not currently reconciled in a shared metric.
[MEDIUM] (governance) Neither stakeholder could name who owns model-output accuracy sign-off; assumed it would 'probably fall to compliance.'
[LOW] (change management) Both anticipate clinician skepticism based on a prior failed CDS (clinical decision support) alert rollout in 2022.
Representative Quotes
"We can't be the org that leaks PHI through some vendor's training pipeline. That's the headline we're trying to avoid, not chase." — Chief Information Officer, P01
"If a doctor spends less time typing and more time looking at the patient, I don't care what's under the hood." — VP Clinical Informatics, P02
Recommendations
Facilitate a follow-up session to align on 2-3 shared, measurable success metrics before scoping any pilot.
Document a RACI for AI-output review/sign-off; surface the gap to Compliance directly.
Reference the 2022 CDS alert rollout retro in early clinician-facing research to avoid repeating known failure modes.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Who in Compliance should own model-output sign-off? Schedule follow-up interview.
Request access to 2022 CDS alert rollout post-mortem if it exists.

Understand executive priorities, risk tolerance, and success criteria for the Compass AI modernization program before any tools are scoped.
Method
Method: 1:1 stakeholder interview (60 min, recorded w/ consent, transcript scrubbed)
Researcher: J. Alvarez
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (risk tolerance) Both stakeholders want AI pilots to start in low-PHI-exposure workflows (scheduling, intake) before touching clinical documentation, citing HIPAA audit exposure as the top concern.
[MEDIUM] (success criteria) VP Clinical Informatics defines success as 'reduced documentation time,' while CIO defines success as 'reduced vendor sprawl' — the two are not currently reconciled in a shared metric.
[MEDIUM] (governance) Neither stakeholder could name who owns model-output accuracy sign-off; assumed it would 'probably fall to compliance.'
[LOW] (change management) Both anticipate clinician skepticism based on a prior failed CDS (clinical decision support) alert rollout in 2022.
Representative Quotes
"We can't be the org that leaks PHI through some vendor's training pipeline. That's the headline we're trying to avoid, not chase." — Chief Information Officer, P01
"If a doctor spends less time typing and more time looking at the patient, I don't care what's under the hood." — VP Clinical Informatics, P02
Recommendations
Facilitate a follow-up session to align on 2-3 shared, measurable success metrics before scoping any pilot.
Document a RACI for AI-output review/sign-off; surface the gap to Compliance directly.
Reference the 2022 CDS alert rollout retro in early clinician-facing research to avoid repeating known failure modes.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Who in Compliance should own model-output sign-off? Schedule follow-up interview.
Request access to 2022 CDS alert rollout post-mortem if it exists.

questions.question: How many clinicians assumed their draft was lost when the session locked during dictation?

runs.answer:
All 4 clinicians who were shadowed assumed the draft was lost when the session locked mid-dictation, and all 4 started dictating again after re-authenticating [1]. The draft had in fact survived server-side [1][2].

The original session notes give the figure as "4 of 5 clinicians." A later correction to those notes explains that the session had 5 participants in total: 4 clinicians who were shadowed and 1 IT Security stakeholder who was interviewed but not shadowed [1]. Only the 4 shadowed clinicians went through a lock during dictation, so the result is all 4, not 4 of 5 [1]. The synthesis and the decision rationale both use this corrected reading of "all 4 clinicians" [3][2].

In the current build, the lock freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message [1]. One physician said: "I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." [1]. A later correction reassigns that quote from P31 to P119 [1].

A separate April 2026 interview with one nurse practitioner (P148) describes the same pattern from their own past [4]. They said they once re-dictated a visit summary early on and then found the original draft intact [4]. Now they re-authenticate and scroll through the draft before saying anything more [4]. This is their own account of their practice, not an observed behavior [4].

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

runs.answer:

Because only the 4 clinicians went through a lock during dictation, the correct result is all 4 of 4 [1]. The synthesis and decision rationale also state the figure as all 4 shadowed clinicians [3][2].

The cause was that a lock mid-recording froze the ambient-scribe widget with no message [1]. Participants could not tell "recording," "frozen because locked" and "actually stopped" apart [1]. They described re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact [4]. They now re-authenticate and scroll through the draft before saying more [4]. questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

runs.answer:
The biggest documented pain point is the sheer burden of documentation. In the September 2025 baseline survey of 287 clinicians, physicians ranked documentation as their #1 contributor to burnout (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. In the same survey, 64% of physicians reported regularly charting after hours ("pajama time"), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours a day [1]. One physician wrote, "I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed" [1]. Respondents knew the survey related to an AI initiative, which may have shaped their answers [1]. A nurse practitioner also warned that AI shouldn't become "the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it" [1].

Since the ambient scribe launched, single-participant interviews point to newer, narrower pain points:

- Scribe-drafted notes read as complete, so missing acuity, severity and clinical indicators are harder to spot. A CDI specialist estimated each note now takes a few extra minutes to review: "The note sounds finished. That's the problem." [2]
- Coders can't see when a CDI query is already open, which leads to premature coding or duplicate physician queries. This problem predates the scribe [2].
- A rheumatologist must read all of a long medication list ("fifteen lines, give or take") because changed lines look the same as lines that were only mentioned [3].
- Drafts sometimes drop the later steps of a taper or leave "weekly" off methotrexate, and these errors aren't underlined [3].
- A dose the patient reported can read like the clinician's decision [3].

Among nurses in February 2025, the top concern about AI documentation was losing their clinical narrative voice [4].

sources.title: Interview — CDI Specialist on Documentation Gaps in AI-Drafted Notes
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P123 — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist (him-coder) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how scribe-drafted notes have changed clinical documentation integrity (CDI) review since the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, and how a CDI specialist would want the AI coding-suggestion concept (July 2025 prototype, not built or piloted) to behave when the documentation behind a code is incomplete.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant does concurrent and retrospective CDI review on inpatient and some outpatient encounters and writes physician queries. They work alongside the coding team but sit in a separate queue.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes are fluent and well organized, so they read as complete. What's missing (acuity, severity, the clinical indicators that support a diagnosis, the link between conditions) is harder to spot than in a sparse typed note, where a gap was obvious at a glance. They said a scribe-drafted note now takes a more deliberate read, by their own informal count a few extra minutes per note, because they can no longer rely on a note "looking thin" to tell them where to look.
[MEDIUM] (queries) Wants the coding-suggestion concept to suggest queries, not codes, when the documentation is incomplete. Their worry is that a suggested code on an under-specified note pushes the coder either to an unspecified code or toward a leading query. They'd want a draft query that states the clinical indicators found and asks the physician to clarify, in non-leading language Compliance has approved.
[LOW] (workflow) There is no hand-off signal between CDI and coding. Coders can't see that a CDI query is already open on an encounter, so an encounter sometimes gets coded before the answer comes back, or the physician gets a second, near-duplicate query from the coder. They described this as an annoyance that predates the scribe, not something GA caused.
Representative Quotes
"The note sounds finished. That's the problem. It reads like a really good note, and then you go looking for the acuity and it's just not in there." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
"Don't hand me a code. Hand me the question I should be asking the doctor." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
Recommendations
For under-specified documentation, have the coding-suggestion concept output a draft query routed to CDI instead of a code, with query wording reviewed by Compliance so it stays non-leading.
Share CDI's list of the specificity elements most often missing from scribe-drafted notes with the ambient scribe team, alongside the coders' list.
Separately from any AI work, look at a simple "query open" indicator on the encounter that coders can see.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with Compliance which query templates are already approved, and whether AI-drafted query text would need its own review.
Get CDI query counts for the months before and after GA.

sources.title: Interview — Rheumatologist on Medication Lines in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2 (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:30; 2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:31), sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31), and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:21-27). Since GA, a family physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic described checking each medication change in the plan against the order they had placed (2026-03-24-interview-family-physician-plan-and-medication-changes-at-sign-off/session-notes.md:28, :32). No raw session dated on or before this one mentions a specialty clinic, rheumatology, a dose taper or a weekly dosing schedule. This session asked a rheumatologist, about six months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the medication lines in a draft when a patient's medication list is long and doses change often.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a rheumatologist in an ambulatory specialty clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no medication-specific marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (long lists) Many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (dose schedules) In their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression.
[MEDIUM] (whose dose) Patients often say what they actually take, which can differ from what was prescribed ("I've been taking half"). The draft records the dose that was said without saying who said it, so a patient's report can read like the clinician's decision. They check whether each dose in the draft is what the patient reported or what they decided, and reword it so the note says which. This is one rheumatologist's practice; whether other clinicians make the same check is not known.
[LOW] (what would help) Asked what would help, without being shown anything, they said a way to see which medication lines changed at this visit. That is an expectation; nothing was shown, and the distinct medication flag was not discussed with them.
Representative Quotes
"Fifteen medications and one of them changed today. The draft doesn't tell me which one, so I read all fifteen." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
"It got the first dose right. The rest of the taper just isn't there." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this rheumatologist's account, multi-step dose schedules (tapers, weekly dosing) are where medication lines go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, include specialty-clinic visits with long medication lists and multi-step dose schedules, not only single dose changes.
Explore, as an open design question, whether a draft could show which medication lines changed at this visit and whether a dose is the patient's report or the clinician's decision; neither has been designed or tested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often a dose schedule is written incompletely is not measured; "a few times a month" is one rheumatologist's impression.
Whether other specialists, or NPs and PAs in specialty clinics, check medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag, which targets sound-alike names, would help with dose schedules is untested; it has not shipped.

sources.title: Interview — Rheumatologist on Medication Lines in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2 (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:30; 2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:31), sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31), and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:21-27). Since GA, a family physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic described checking each medication change in the plan against the order they had placed (2026-03-24-interview-family-physician-plan-and-medication-changes-at-sign-off/session-notes.md:28, :32). No raw session dated on or before this one mentions a specialty clinic, rheumatology, a dose taper or a weekly dosing schedule. This session asked a rheumatologist, about six months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the medication lines in a draft when a patient's medication list is long and doses change often.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a rheumatologist in an ambulatory specialty clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no medication-specific marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (long lists) Many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (dose schedules) In their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression.
[MEDIUM] (whose dose) Patients often say what they actually take, which can differ from what was prescribed ("I've been taking half"). The draft records the dose that was said without saying who said it, so a patient's report can read like the clinician's decision. They check whether each dose in the draft is what the patient reported or what they decided, and reword it so the note says which. This is one rheumatologist's practice; whether other clinicians make the same check is not known.
[LOW] (what would help) Asked what would help, without being shown anything, they said a way to see which medication lines changed at this visit. That is an expectation; nothing was shown, and the distinct medication flag was not discussed with them.
Representative Quotes
"Fifteen medications and one of them changed today. The draft doesn't tell me which one, so I read all fifteen." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
"It got the first dose right. The rest of the taper just isn't there." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149

Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this rheumatologist's account, multi-step dose schedules (tapers, weekly dosing) are where medication lines go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, include specialty-clinic visits with long medication lists and multi-step dose schedules, not only single dose changes.
Explore, as an open design question, whether a draft could show which medication lines changed at this visit and whether a dose is the patient's report or the clinician's decision; neither has been designed or tested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often a dose schedule is written incompletely is not measured; "a few times a month" is one rheumatologist's impression.
Whether other specialists, or NPs and PAs in specialty clinics, check medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag, which targets sound-alike names, would help with dose schedules is untested; it has not shipped.

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

runs.answer:
The sources don't show physicians broadly distrusting the scribe. They show trust that grew during testing but stayed partial and section-dependent, with specific reasons for continued careful review.

- Trust was slow to build in testing: In v0.1, P09 said they had to read every word. In v0.2 they said getting it right once didn't mean they trusted it yet [1]. By the GA release-candidate round, P09 skimmed a section for the first time because the underline showed where to look, and 4 of 6 participants said per-line highlighting let them skim high-confidence lines [1][2].
- Errors the underline doesn't flag: In September 2026, P09 said most of their edits now fix the order of events in the history, such as which symptom came first. These lines usually aren't underlined because each word was heard clearly ("a few notes most weeks") [1]. After catching one such draft, they began reading the whole history for new problems. They also read the assessment and plan in full on every draft: "Not the plan, and not the history of a new problem" [1].
- Incidental content: P146 removes small talk, remarks about relatives and their own asides from "most visits, a line or two." They read the whole draft because this accurately transcribed content isn't underlined: "It heard the small talk perfectly, so nothing tells me to look there" [3].
- Clinically important errors: A persona goal, inferred from one session, is catching medication-name errors specifically [4].
- A non-trust reason for hesitancy: One resident didn't opt in at GA because writing their own notes was how they worked out their assessment, not because they doubted the draft's accuracy [5].

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe research looked at what the scribe gets wrong: medication dosages and sound-alike drug names, and whether clinicians trust the draft enough to skim it. Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most of their visits. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (incidental content) Their drafts regularly contain things that were said in the room but that they would not have written themselves: small talk at the start of the visit, a patient's remarks about a relative's health, comments made by a family member who came to the visit, and their own asides ("let me pull up your labs"). They remove these line by line with the in-place edit before signing. They put it at "most visits, a line or two", an informal impression, not a count.
[MEDIUM] (not underlined) The underline marks lines where the scribe was unsure what it heard. Incidental content is usually transcribed accurately, so it is not underlined, and nothing in the draft points them to it. It also doesn't land in a predictable section: they have found it in the history of present illness and in the social history. To catch it they read the whole draft, including sections where nothing is underlined. That is one physician's practice; whether others do the same is not known.
[MEDIUM] (judgement) What counts as incidental is a judgement call. A remark about stress at home can be clinically relevant and stay in the note; the same remark in passing about someone else is removed. They would not want the scribe to remove anything on its own. They could see value in it pointing out lines that might not belong, as long as they decide. That is an expectation; nothing was shown.
Representative Quotes
"It writes down everything that was said, not everything that matters. The sister's surgery is in my note until I take it out." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
"The underline tells me where it wasn't sure what it heard. It heard the small talk perfectly, so nothing tells me to look there." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that the confidence underline doesn't help with incidental content, because that content is usually transcribed accurately; reviewing for it means reading the whole draft.
If anything is designed for this, explore pointing out lines that may not belong in the note rather than removing them, so the clinician makes the call.
Keep this separate from the transcription-confidence work: it is about what belongs in the note, not whether it was heard correctly.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often drafts contain incidental content is not measured; "most visits, a line or two" is one physician's impression.
Whether other physicians, NPs and PAs remove the same kinds of content, and how long it takes them, is not known; this is one interview.
What happens to text a clinician removes before signing is not recorded in the corpus and was not discussed in this session.
